accuracy.evidence: Exact values checked against the UK Weights and Measures Act 1985 (Schedule 1) and NIST Handbook 44 Appendix C: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 pound = 0.45359237 kg (so 1 kg = 2.2046 lb), 1 UK pint = 568.261 ml (so 1 litre = 1.7598 UK pints), 1 US liquid pint = 473.176 ml. The lab computes from the exact values and shows them beside the rough rules: 4 in = 10.2 cm, 12 in = 30.5 cm, 11 lb = 4.99 kg, 7 pints = 3.98 L, 7 lb ÷ 2.2 ≈ 3.2 kg (exact 3.18), 12-inch pizza = 30.5 cm, 6 pints = 3.4 L, 40 in = 101.6 cm. The rough rules 2.5, 2.2 and 1.75 are those used in the NC Year 5 non-statutory guidance and White Rose Maths. Parameterised answers (2.5n, 2.2n, 2n, 1.75n, 5n) were enumerated by the validator and are exact to 2 dp.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors reported in NCETM and White Rose Maths guidance on converting units: multiplying when you should divide (7-pound baby as 15 kg in p3, est step feedback, challenge tag wrongway, distractors in m5 and m6), 'the number stays the same' (m8, step 2 predict 'They weigh the same', challenge tag same), adding the rate (tag add, distractors 24 kg and 42 cm), flipping the rule to 1 lb ≈ 2.2 kg (sorter card, tag flip), and 1 inch ≈ 1 cm or 10 cm (step 1 predict, tags same and tenfold). Each wrong answer gets its own message.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed. Nearby labs are 875 Converting measurement units (flagconv: metric-to-metric ×/÷ 10, 100, 1000), 597 Choosing measurement units (flagunits) and 916 Energy bills (flagkwh). None compares metric with imperial: this lab has a double cm/inch ruler, a balance matched with 1 lb weights, a 4-litre bucket filled by UK pints, a × 2.5 / ÷ 2.5 / × 2.2 / ÷ 2.2 sorter and number-line estimates. It could not be reused by relabelling.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners find each rule by measuring before it is stated: the pencil readout shows 4 in = 10.2 cm and 12 in = 30.5 cm side by side on two scales; the beam only levels at 11 one-pound weights against 5 kg, giving 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb; the bucket only fills at 7 pints, giving 1 L ≈ 1.75 pints; the sorter feedback names the size check (smaller unit means more of them, so multiply) and the estimate step makes them use it. The banner states the rule only after each task is won.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Which is longer, 1 cm or 1 inch?' with 'They are the same'; '1 kg bag or 1 lb block, which is heavier?' with 'the 1 lb block' and 'the same' (the same-number belief); 'How many pints fill 4 litres?' with '4 pints' (same number) and 'about 2' (flipped rule). The ruler, balance and bucket then show the answer and the task message reports the prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with tagged wrong options and specific feedback: same (an inch is about 2.5 cm), tenfold (far too big, use the rough rules), flip (1 of the bigger unit is more than 1 of the smaller), wrongway (to a bigger unit the number gets smaller, so divide; to a smaller unit multiply) and add (converting is × or ÷, never adding the rule). Correct answers build a streak.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores Flesch-Kincaid 2.7 (limit 6.5) and adult text 4.2 (limit 9.5). Metric, imperial, inch, pound, pint, kilogram and litre are introduced with everyday examples (TV sizes, baby weights, milk), the ≈ sign is always read alongside 'about', and buttons are plain ('Longer by ¼ inch', 'Add a 1 lb weight', 'Pour in 1 pint', 'Check my estimate').

no_filler.evidence: gate_content found no filler phrases and the explanation shares under 12% of 6-word shingles with every other lesson. Each kid paragraph does one job (the two unit families, the three rough rules, multiply or divide, estimating and sense-checking); the adult text gives the standard, exact values with sources, the task list and common mistakes, including the UK/US pint difference.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px screenshots in light and dark themes before and after Show me at every step (/workspace/shots/imp-*, impd-*). After the first pass the 1 L jug and pint glass were stacked from the top of the panel (the jug label was clipped above the panel) and the number-line instruction was shortened (it ran off both edges at 360 px). Inch labels show every 2 inches on phones so they do not collide; the ruler, balance, bucket, rule boxes and number line fit without clipping, and every action has a full-width button.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all five tasks complete with Show me, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes and there are no console errors. Every drag has button equivalents (Longer/Shorter by 1 or ¼ inch, Add a 1 lb weight / Take a weight off, Pour in 1 pint, Pick then rule, Arrow up/down and Check my estimate), the canvas aria-label states the live values (inches and cm, pounds and kg on the pan, pints and litres in the bucket, cards sorted, arrow position), and feedback is announced through c.say.
